purpose: Dexmedetomidine is used to help people feel calm, relaxed, and sleepy, especially when they are in the hospital or intensive care unit (ICU). It is also used to keep patients comfortable and sedated while on a breathing machine or during certain medical procedures. A newer form that dissolves under the tongue is used to help calm people during episodes of agitation related to certain mental health conditions.
how_it_works: This medicine works by attaching to certain receptors in your brain and nervous system called alpha-2 receptors. When it activates these receptors, it slows down the signals that cause anxiety, stress, and wakefulness, helping you feel calm and drowsy. Unlike some other sedatives, it lets you stay somewhat responsive, meaning doctors can still wake you up and talk to you if needed.
common_side_effects: Low blood pressure (you may feel dizzy or lightheaded), slow heart rate, dry mouth, nausea, and feeling very sleepy or groggy. Some people also experience brief high blood pressure right when the medicine is first given.
warnings: This medicine can cause your blood pressure and heart rate to drop to dangerously low levels, so your medical team will monitor you closely. It should not be stopped suddenly if used for a long time, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, low blood pressure, liver disease, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. It is only given in a medical setting by trained healthcare professionals.
typical_dosing: When given through an IV in the hospital, dosing is carefully adjusted by your medical team based on your weight and how sedated you need to be — there is no one-size-fits-all dose. The under-the-tongue film (Igalmi) is typically given as a single dose of 120 or 180 micrograms, and your doctor decides the right amount for you. You will always be monitored by healthcare staff whenever this medicine is used.
